title: Exploring the impact of music on response to ketamine/esketamine: A scoping review

claims.statement: As described in one scoping review (Kheirkhah et al., 2024; searched to December 2023; the included studies were not appraised, so its figures are second-hand), evidence is insufficient to say whether music changes how a ketamine or esketamine session goes. The review found 14 studies of music with ketamine, all in clinical settings. In nine, ketamine was given with other sedatives or painkillers during procedures; in most of them music went with less sedation or drug use and lower anxiety, pain or fear, but one trial found no effect on emergence reactions and another found more dreams or emergence reactions with music, though no unpleasant dreams, against 10 controls with unpleasant dreams. Of the five studies of ketamine or esketamine alone, the only one with a comparison group was in 46 children having heart catheterization under ketamine anaesthesia: the 23 who heard recordings of their mothers' voices (musical in 12 of them) had less anxiety before the procedure and fewer emergence reactions than 23 who wore headphones with no recording. The other four were case reports and interview studies: a woman on esketamine nasal spray found that music of her choice helped with dissociation, confusion and anxiety; two patients with bipolar depression tolerated dissociation better with preferred music in later infusions, which may reflect getting used to the infusions; in 12 people given ketamine in a trial for alcohol use disorder, everyone who listened to music heard it distorted in speed and pitch, felt as good or bad depending on their state; and of 17 people on esketamine for depression, one stopped using music because it kept him tied to the outside world. No controlled study tested music during ketamine or esketamine treatment for depression, and the review's own limitations say no conclusions can be drawn. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: No pooled estimates. 14 studies: 9 with other sedatives (music with less sedation and lower anxiety or pain in most; no effect on emergence reactions in one; more dreams or emergence reactions in another); 5 with ketamine or esketamine alone, one controlled (46 children: mothers' voices against a blank recording), the rest case reports (3 patients) and interview studies (17 and 12 people). No controlled study of music with ketamine for depression.
